quote: Suche die Invariante einer Punktmenge d.h. man soll ein allgemeines Gesetz finden, welches mir gestattet, aus jeder beliebig geg. Punktmenge einen bestimmten Punkt heraus- zugreifen
english: Find the invariant of a point set, i.e. one should find a general law which allows me to pick out a definite point from any arbitrarily given point set.
topic: Notes on difference operators and iterated integrals, a proof that a continuous function whose difference f(x+a)-f(x) is independent of x is linear, a related argument using the integral F of f, and a problem of finding an invariant of a point set that singles out a particular point.

triage.modern_statement: Find an explicit choice function on the point sets of R (or R^n): a single rule F that assigns to every nonempty set A of points a definite point F(A) in A. For arbitrary sets this amounts to an explicit well-ordering of the continuum, since 'take the least element' then gives the rule. Modern framing: (a) Is there such a function at all? With the Axiom of Choice, yes, and this is equivalent to the reals being well-orderable. (b) Can one be explicitly defined without AC, in ZF? No. It is consistent with ZF that the reals have no well-ordering, so ZF cannot prove one exists, let alone give a definable one. For restricted classes, such as closed sets, one can write explicit rules, for example the lexicographically least point of a nonempty closed bounded set.
triage.answered_by: Ernst Zermelo, in a letter to Hilbert dated 24 Sept 1904 and published in Math. Annalen 1904. He proved that every set can be well-ordered by assuming a choice principle, later named the Axiom of Choice. Read literally, the question asks whether such a 'law' can be constructed, and the negative answer comes from later independence results: Cohen-style forcing models of ZF in which the reals cannot be well-ordered (Feferman, Solovay and others in the 1960s). Hilbert later built this kind of choice operator into his own logic as the epsilon operator (1920s).

evidence.claim: Zermelo published a proof of the well-ordering theorem in 1904 as an extract from a letter to Hilbert, and that proof is where he first introduced the 'choice' principle.
On 24 September 1904 Zermelo sent Hilbert a letter proving the well-ordering theorem from what he later called the axiom of choice.

Hilbert suggested, in connection with the continuum problem (his 1st Paris problem, 1900), that one should first prove Cantor's conjecture that every set can be well-ordered. Zermelo took this first step in 1904.
Hilbert's epsilon calculus has a term-forming operator that picks a witness. It is read as a logical choice operator, and its semantics are given by choice functions on the power set of the universe.
ZF does not give a definable well-order, and it is consistent with ZF that the reals cannot be well-ordered (there are models of ZF with no well-ordering of the reals).

triage.why: Choosing 'a definite point from any arbitrarily given point set' by a general law is exactly the choice-function / well-ordering problem for the continuum. Hilbert himself raised the well-ordering of the continuum in the 1900 statement of his 1st problem. Zermelo settled it in 1904, in a letter to Hilbert, by postulating AC, and independence results later showed that no such law can be explicitly given or proved to exist in ZF alone. So the question is resolved and is foundational, not an open research area, although definable well-orderings are still studied in descriptive set theory. Confidence is medium rather than high for three reasons. First, the note's wording ('Invariante') is vague. Second, I could not determine the page's date relative to 1904. Third, I am linking an undated notebook note to the 1st problem and AC by interpretation; no source discusses this notebook entry directly. None of the search results named Feferman or Solovay, so the 1960s attribution is from background knowledge, not a cited source.
